lessons.title: Chasing Happiness Makes You Less Happy
lessons.key_idea: Wanting a positive experience is itself a negative experience, so accepting the negative is what actually frees you.

lessons.title: Choose Your Problems, Not Problem-Free Life
lessons.key_idea: Life is never free of problems, so happiness comes from choosing struggles you enjoy and solving them.

lessons.title: You Are Not Special
lessons.key_idea: Believing you are exceptional, whether great or uniquely broken, is entitlement that stops you from growing.

lessons.title: Pick Better Values to Measure Yourself
lessons.key_idea: Your suffering depends on your values, so trade shallow ones like pleasure and popularity for ones you control, like honesty and growth.

lessons.title: Responsibility Is Not the Same as Fault
lessons.key_idea: Even when something isn't your fault, you are always responsible for how you respond to it.

lessons.title: Failure Is the Way Forward
lessons.key_idea: Action creates motivation, so doing something small, even badly, beats waiting to feel ready.

lessons.title: Saying No and Remembering Death
lessons.key_idea: Committing to a few things by rejecting the rest, and remembering life is short, shows what is truly worth caring about.

plan.title: The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck
plan.author: Mark Manson
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's chapters, core arguments and main examples in good detail, though I may not recall every minor anecdote precisely.
plan.one_liner: A good life isn't about caring less. It's about caring only about what truly matters.
plan.summary: Mark Manson argues that modern self-help has it backwards. Constantly chasing positivity and success only reminds us of what we lack. He says we all have a limited amount of attention and concern, so the real skill is choosing carefully what deserves it. Life will always bring problems. Happiness comes from picking good problems and enjoying the work of solving them. Manson takes aim at entitlement, the belief that we are special and deserve to feel good all the time. He urges us to adopt better values, take responsibility for everything in our lives even when it isn't our fault, doubt our own certainty, and treat failure as the path to growth. Finally, he argues that facing our own mortality helps us see clearly what is truly worth caring about.
